raw_case_text:
A 20-year-old male patient sought the emergency unit complaining of high-grade fever and chills accompanied by malaise, headache, and weakness during the last 10 days. He referred loss of appetite and consequently 3 kg of weight loss (5% of total body weight). His physical examination was normal, as well as the ophthalmoscopy. Laboratory workup showed normal renal function, glucose determination, electrolytes, hepatic enzymes, liver function tests, protein electrophoresis, and urinalysis. Serology for HIV, hepatitis B and C, toxoplasmosis, EBV, syphilis, leptospirosis, and dengue fever were negative. Rubella and cytomegalovirus serologies showed IgG positive but IgM negative. Tests for antinuclear antibody, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, and rheumatoid factor were also negative. The tuberculin skin test was negative as well as the acid-fast bacilli research in the sputum. The thoracic CT was normal and echodoppler of the lower limbs ruled out the diagnosis of deep venous thrombosis. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination was normal. Four sets of blood samples, urine, and CSF cultures were negative for bacteria, fungus, and acid-fast bacilli. The patient remained hospitalized presenting a daily temperature of 38.5  C and 39  C and was recorded as a fever of unknown origin (FUO). In this setting, he underwent a transesophageal echodopplercardiogram, which was normal. The determination of a high titer of ferritin was odd, which was interpreted as an inflammatory marker or even the possibility of Still's disease, without other diagnostic criteria. The abdominal ultrasound and CT were normal despite the progressive raising determination of liver enzymes (AST, ALT, APh and gammaGT) and LDHi. Nevertheless he was submitted to a wedge liver biopsy through laparoscopy, which did not detect any abnormality in the abdominal cavity. The histological examination of the liver specimen showed non-specific findings: preserved lobular architecture, with moderate neutrophilic infiltration of portal tract with histiocytes, mild biliary ductal proliferation. The hepatocytes, Kupfer cells, as well as the central veins were also preserved. Bone marrow aspiration resulted in dry tap, which was followed by a bone marrow biopsy, which showed hypoplasia of the all hematopoietic series and focal infiltration by large lymphoid cells, with nuclear pleomorphism, atypia and evident nucleoli.
The patient evolved with lower limb cellulitis and septic shock, and died before the complete diagnostic work up has been completed. Unfortunately the bone marrow biopsy was not prioritized over the other examinations, being undertaken lately in the course of the disease. The diagnosis was confirmed by the immunohistochemical report, which showed a profile consistent with ALK+ ALCL: (positive for CD30, ALK, and EMA, and negative for CD20, CD3, CD15, CD43, CD34, CD31, and myeloperoxidase) (Figure 2).
The autopsy revealed generalized lymphadenopathy (lymph nodes measuring up to 2 cm) involving the axillary, mediastinal, abdominal, and lower limb chains, which showed sinusoidal infiltration by large, atypical multinucleated cells (Figure 3).
The lungs, liver, and spleen also showed lymphomatous infiltration (Figure 4). The final diagnosis was ALK+ ALCL and the immediate cause of death was septic shock with massive bilateral pulmonary hemorrhage.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 20-year-old male presented with a 10-day history of high-grade fever, chills, malaise, headache, generalized weakness, anorexia, and a 3 kg weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with 10 days of daily high-grade fevers (38.5-39 C), chills, malaise, headache, weakness, anorexia, and 5% body weight loss (3 kg). During prolonged hospitalization for fever of unknown origin, he developed progressive transaminitis, hyperferritinemia, lower-limb cellulitis, and fatal septic shock with massive pulmonary hemorrhage.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for daily high-grade fever (38.5-39 C), chills, malaise, headache, weakness, loss of appetite, and 3 kg weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: Initial physical examination and ophthalmoscopy were completely normal; persistently febrile (38.5-39 C daily) during hospitalization, later developing lower-limb cellulitis and septic shock.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial renal function, glucose, electrolytes, liver enzymes, protein electrophoresis, and urinalysis were normal, followed by progressively rising AST, ALT, ALP, GGT, LDH, and markedly elevated serum ferritin. Serologies for HIV, HBV, HCV, toxoplasmosis, EBV, syphilis, and leptospirosis were negative (rubella and CMV IgG+ / IgM-); ANA, ANCA, RF, tuberculin skin test, sputum AFB, and 4 sets of blood, urine, and CSF cultures were negative. Lower-limb Doppler ultrasound, abdominal ultrasound, and transesophageal echocardiogram were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic CT, abdominal CT, and CSF analysis were normal. Laparoscopic wedge liver biopsy showed preserved lobular architecture with moderate portal neutrophilic/histiocytic infiltration and mild biliary ductular proliferation. Bone marrow aspiration yielded a dry tap, and trephine bone marrow biopsy plus autopsy revealed hypoplasia with focal infiltration by large pleomorphic lymphoid cells (CD30+, ALK+, EMA+, negative for CD20, CD3, CD15, CD43, CD34, CD31, MPO) and disseminated lymphomatous involvement of axillary, mediastinal, abdominal, and lower-limb lymph nodes, lungs, liver, and spleen.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: ALK-positive anaplastic large-cell lymphoma (ALK+ ALCL) presenting as fever of unknown origin with bone marrow, nodal, hepatic, splenic, and pulmonary infiltration, confirmed by bone marrow biopsy immunohistochemistry (CD30+, ALK+, EMA+) and autopsy. Dengue fever was ruled out by negative dengue serology. The patient died of septic shock and massive bilateral pulmonary hemorrhage before targeted lymphoma chemotherapy could be initiated.
